fields.complete_source:
Solution
Proof. Let e = {x, y} be an arbitrary edge in T1. Since T1 is a tree, removing e disconnects T1 into
exactly two components (each of which is itself a tree). Denote these components by A and B, with
vertex sets VA and VB respectively, such that x ∈VA and y ∈VB. (Equivalently, VA and VB form a
partition of V , and e was the unique edge of T1 connecting a vertex of VA to a vertex of VB.)
Now, consider the second tree T2. Since T2 is connected, there is a unique path in T2 from x to y.
Write this path as
x = v0 −−v1 −−v2 −−· · · −−vk = y,
where each vi is a vertex in V and each vi −−vi+1 is an edge in T2. Along this path, we move from
x ∈VA to y ∈VB, so there must exist some index j where the path first enters VB. In other words, for
some 1 ≤j ≤k, we have vj−1 ∈VA and vj ∈VB. Consider the edge
f := { vj−1, vj }.
This f is an edge of T2 (since it lies on the T2–path from x to y) and, by construction, one endpoint of
f lies in VA and the other lies in VB. Moreover, f cannot belong to T1 (otherwise T1 would contain an
edge directly connecting VA and VB other than e, which contradicts the fact that removing e disconnects
T1).
Now we exchange the edges e and f between the two graphs. Define the modified edge sets
E′
1 := (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f},
E′
2 := (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e},
and let T ′
1 = (V, E′
1) and T ′
2 = (V, E′
2) be the resulting graphs. We claim that both T ′
1 and T ′
2 are trees.
**1. T ′
1 is a tree:** T ′
1 has |E′
1| = |T1| = |V | −1 edges (since we removed one edge from T1 and
added one edge). We need to check T ′
1 is connected and acyclic. By construction, T1 \ {e} consisted
of two disjoint trees A and B. The new edge f = {vj−1, vj} added to E′
1 directly connects a vertex
vj−1 ∈VA to a vertex vj ∈VB. Thus, f reconnects A and B, making T ′
1 a connected graph on all of V .
Furthermore, T ′
1 has no cycles: removing e broke all paths between VA and VB in T1, so there was no
path in A ∪B between vj−1 and vj; hence adding the single edge f = {vj−1, vj} cannot create a cycle
(it simply provides the unique route between VA and VB in T ′
1). In summary, T ′
1 is connected and has
|V | −1 edges with no cycles, which means T ′
1 is a spanning tree on V .
**2. T ′
2 is a tree:** Analogously, T ′
2 has |E′
2| = |T2| = |V | −1 edges. Since T2 was a tree, removing
f disconnects T2 into two components. Notably, f = {vj−1, vj} lay on the unique T2–path from x to y,
so after deleting f, the vertices x and y become separated into different components of T2 \ {f}. The
added edge e = {x, y} in E′
2 precisely reconnects those two components by joining x and y. Thus T ′
2 is
again a connected graph covering all vertices. Moreover, no cycle is created by adding e, since in T2 \{f}
there was no longer any path between x and y (if there were, T2 would have had two distinct x–y paths
originally, contradicting the uniqueness of paths in a tree). Therefore T ′
2 is also connected and acyclic
with |V | −1 edges, i.e. a tree.
In conclusion, for the chosen edge e ∈T1 we have found an edge f ∈T2 such that swapping e and f
yields two new trees T ′
1 and T ′
2. This proves the required statement: for every edge e ∈T1, there exists
an edge f ∈T2 such that (V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) and (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) are both trees.
1

fields.problem:
Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 36
Suppose that (V, T1) and (V, T2) are two trees defined over a common vertex set V . Prove
that for every edge e in the edge set T1, there exists a corresponding edge f in T2 such
that exchanging these edges preserves the tree structure for both graphs; that is, prove
that (V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) and (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) are both trees.
1

Take V={a,b}, T1=T2 with the single edge e={a,b}. Removing e from T1 gives components A={a}, B={b}. The unique T2 path from a to b is just the edge {a,b}, so the constructed f is {a,b}=e, which is in T1. Thus the local claim 'f cannot belong to T1' is false, although the main exchange statement still holds in this instance.
